study.title: Job 15 - Eliphaz insists that the righteous sufferer is a hidden sinner
study.overview: In this chapter, Eliphaz again attacks Job with harsh language and assumes that suffering is a sure proof of guilt. First, he reproves Job's speech as empty and irreverent, as if Job was despising wisdom and prayer. Then Eliphaz exalts the superiority of the older and presents a severe view of the human condition: no one would be pure before God, let alone the common human being. Finally, he describes the fate of the wicked as distressing, unstable and frustrated, culminating in the strong image that wickedness is conceived and generated from the inside, until it produces deception. The chapter, thus, is less a consolation and another theological accusation against Job.

outline.title: Eliphaz accuses Job of speaking without wisdom and treating God with irreverence
outline.explanation: Eliphaz begins by disqualifying Job's speech as useless words. He accuses him of despising the fear of God, of rejecting prayer and speaking as one dominated by wickedness. He then insists that Job cannot stand above the tradition of the older or above collective wisdom, and concludes that the human being, in general, is not pure before God.

outline.title: Eliphaz presents tradition about the fate of the wicked
outline.explanation: Eliphaz states that what will say comes from the observation of the wise and the testimony of the ancients. He describes the wicked as one whose life is marked by fear, threat, anguish, and ruin, especially because he stood up against God. The image is that of false and short prosperity, which is not sustained before the judgment.

outline.title: Evil as a pregnancy of deception
outline.explanation: The chapter ends with a proverbial conclusion: the perverse person conceives wickedness, gives birth to perversity and generates deception. The figure of childbirth shows that sin is not an isolated accident, but fruit produced within the corrupted heart.

study.context: This chapter belongs to the second round of speeches between Job and his friends. The notes indicate that, in this period, friends begin to insist more strongly on the idea that suffering reveals moral guilt. Eliphaz speaks as someone who claims the authority of the ancient experience and the wisdom of the older, using this to interpret Job's situation.
study.theology: The chapter presents a partial and severe theology of suffering: It is part of the conviction that the unevitably suffers and therefore concludes that Job must be guilty. His speech contains general truths about human corruption, the futility of arrogance before God and the seriousness of sin; but in the context of the book these truths are improperly applied to Job. The text also highlights the distance between the holiness of God and the human condition: neither heavenly beings would be pure before him, the more corrupt man. At the same time, the chapter shows the danger of turning moral observations into infallible sentence on someone else's life. In spiritual terms, the root of evil appears as something gestated internally, showing that sin is not only external behavior, but deep inclination of the heart.

scholarViews.insight: Eliphaz uses the image of the eastern wind to call Job's speech empty and aggressive, as a speech without substance.
Eliphaz is offended because Job did not accept their assessment; therefore, he treats him as a stubborn and unjustly accused of many evils.
The final image of the chapter describes wickedness as an inner conception that, after being gestated, gives birth to deceit; sin is presented as a corrupt childbirth.

questions: At what times can I be confusing religious convictions with hasty judgment about another person?
How to distinguish a general biblical truth from a wrong application of this truth to someone's situation?
What signs show that my heart is generating deception even before my words and attitudes appear?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine the very tendency to speak with certainty where there should be humility. Instead of using someone's pain as an automatic guilt test, the Christian is invited to listen carefully, to speak with fear before God and to remember that the human heart can produce deception. In practice, this means avoiding quick conclusions about the suffering of others, cultivating compassion before accusation and asking God to reveal any evil hidden inside.
study.uncertainty: The chapter brings the words of Eliphaz, not the final evaluation of the book on Job. The notes provided allow to safely affirm the accusatory intention of Elifaz and his retributive theology, but do not allow to detail beyond the historical context, the authorship of the discourse or conclude that the generalizations of Elifaz are the complete truth about Job's case.
